title: 𓂋𓄿 𓏌𓅱 𓉐𓂋𓏏𓂻 𓅓 𓉔𓂋𓅱𓇳
titleEn: Book of the Dead of Ani — Spells 61 and 54
part: Spells 61 and 54 — not letting the ba be taken away; giving breath in the necropolis (Plate 15)
work: Book of the Dead of Ani
workEn: Book of the Dead of Ani
draftNote: Draft — the hieroglyphs are read from the printed type of Budge's 1895 edition of the papyrus, and the signs and readings are still being checked; expect changes.
source: Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA 10470), Plate XV. Hieroglyphs transcribed from the interlinear text of E. A. W. Budge, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum (London, 1895), pp. 91–95; Budge's transliteration and word-by-word English were used to check the reading of the signs and the sense, never for wording. Only the papyrus's own text is given: the passages Budge supplies from other papyri in his appendixes and footnotes are left out. Transliteration in the Leiden convention, with the reed written i; translation made fresh from the Egyptian. Shown left to right; the papyrus is written in columns read from the top down. The line under each word ("say") is the conventional Egyptological classroom pronunciation — a neutral e between consonants; ꜣ and ꜥ as a; w as u or w; ṯ as tj; ḏ as dj; ḫ and ẖ as kh; š as sh — an artificial teaching pronunciation, since the vowels of Egyptian were never written. The grouping of signs within a word follows Budge's type, which regularises the scribe's hand.
about: Two short spells on Plate 15 of Ani's papyrus, written after Spells 26 and 30B. In Spell 61 Ani speaks as one who came forth from the flood, so that his ba shall not be taken from him in the necropolis. In Spell 54 he is given breath there: he is the egg of the Great Cackler, a goose of the beginning of things, and its guardian, and he lives and breathes the air. Budge prints chapters from other papyri between and after the two spells, which are left out; several words here are rare or doubtful, and the notes say so.

sentences.l: spell · of · not · letting · be-taken-away · the-ba · of-a-man · from-him · in · the-necropolis
sentences.i: Spell for not letting a man's ba be taken away from him in the necropolis.
sentences.n: Spell 61 begins. The papyrus writes rꜣ n tm rdit nḥm·tw in red, then bꜣ s in black, m-ꜥ·f in red again, and m ẖrt-nṯr in black. rꜣ n 'spell of' is the mouth with its stroke and water n, as in every title. tm is t, the sledge tm (U15) and the sign m (Aa15) as complement, with the t written first, as in Spell 30B: the negative verb 'not to do'. rdit after it is the mouth r, the arm (D36; no loaf is printed) and t: the negatival complement, written with t, 'not letting'. nḥm·tw is water n and the well ḥm (coded N41), with m as complement, then t and the chick w. It is nḥm 'take away' with ·tw, the passive sḏm·tw·f after rdi, 'letting (the ba) be taken away'. bꜣ 'the ba' is the jabiru (G29) with the small bowl (R7) printed at its foot and not read, as in Spell 26. Budge also prints a tiny tick above the bird, which is not coded. s 'man' is the bolt s, a stroke and the seated man (A1). bꜣ s, two nouns side by side, is the direct genitive, 'the ba of a man'. m-ꜥ·f 'from him' is the sign m (Aa15) over the arm ꜥ, and the viper ·f: the compound preposition m-ꜥ 'from (the hand of)', m 'in' with ꜥ 'hand', here written with Aa15 for the owl (Budge: mā-f). ẖrt-nṯr 'the necropolis' is the flag nṯr, written first out of respect, with r (a loop, coded D21, approximate) and the block ẖr (T28), as in Spell 26. The ba is the self that moves freely after death, and to lose it would be to lose life in the next world.

sentences.l: said · by · the-Osiris · the-scribe · Ani · I · it-is · I · the-one-who-came-forth · from · the-flood
sentences.i: Said by the Osiris, the scribe Ani: It is I. I am the one who came forth from the flood.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḏd in in red. ḏd in N 'said by N', as before: the cobra and the hand in one ligature, then the reed and water n. wsir is the eye, the seat and the seated god, and sš 'scribe' is the palette (Budge: ān). ꜣny has a plain seated man (A1) as its classifier here, with no flail. ink 'I' is the ring in (W24) with k and the seated man, as before. ink pw, 'I (am) it', is a sentence on its own: 'it is I'. The second ink opens a nominal sentence, ink N 'I am N'. Budge's line numeral 2 stands before pr, the house pr with r as complement and the walking legs: the participle of pri, 'the one who came forth' (Budge: per). m 'from' is the owl. ꜣgꜣb is the vulture ꜣ, the jar-stand g (W11), a second vulture, the foot b and three lines of water (N35A) as classifier. It is taken as ꜣgb 'flood, flood-water' (Budge: aḳab, 'the water floods'). The second vulture, which Budge also reads, is not explained, and the reading keeps it as it stands. The speaker claims to have been born from the waters, from which all life comes.

sentences.l: has-let-it · flood-my · be-mighty · there · as · the-river
sentences.i: It has let my flood be mighty there, as the river.
sentences.n: rdy·n·f is the mouth r and the arm (D36, again without a loaf), two reeds y, water n and the viper ·f. It is the sḏm·n·f of rdi 'give, let', 'it has let', with the weak y written out (Budge prints it as one group, erṭāi-nef). It could also be split as rdy n·f, the passive participle with n·f, 'to whom … was given'. Its subject 'it' is taken to be the flood of line 1. bꜥḥ·i is the foot b crossed by the arm ꜥ in one ligature, the wick ḥ, a bird on a perch and the seated man ·i: bꜥḥ 'flood, abundance' with 'my'. The bird is coded G7 (the falcon on a standard), approximate. It is more likely the heron on its perch (G32), the classifier with which the Hymn to Ra writes bꜥḥ. sḫm is the sceptre sḫm (S42) with m as complement and the low hooked sign (U15) as classifier, the sign printed for the arm with a stick, the classifier of force: sḫm·i 'I have power' in Spell 30B is written the same way. Budge reads seχem-f, but no viper is printed, and the reading follows the signs: sḫm with no suffix. It is taken as the stative after rdi and its object, 'let my flood (be) mighty'. im 'there' is the reed and the owl, and m 'as' is the owl. itrw 'the river' is the reed, t, r and the chick w. Its classifiers are three lines of water, a canal (N36) and a small strip of land (coded N21, approximate) with a stroke. Who 'it' is, and how the clauses hang together, is not certain. The flood of the Nile was the source of all plenty, and the speaker takes its power for himself. After this unit Budge prints Spells 60, 62, 63A and 63B, with another copy of Spell 61, from Naville's edition of other papyri: Ani's papyrus does not have them, and it goes on with Spell 54.

sentences.l: spell · of · giving · breath · in · the-necropolis
sentences.i: Spell for giving breath in the necropolis.
sentences.n: Spell 54 begins, and Budge's line numerals start again at 1. The papyrus writes rꜣ n rdit nfw m in red; ẖrt-nṯr is black. rdit is the mouth r, t and the arm (D36, no loaf), with t printed above the arm: the infinitive of rdi. nfw 'breath, air' is the sail (P5) with the chick w as complement and a stroke. ẖrt-nṯr is the flag nṯr, the block ẖr (T28) over the loop r (coded D21, approximate), t, and a hill sign (coded N25, approximate) as classifier. This is the fuller writing, with the t of ẖrt. Breath is life, and the dead man asks to breathe again in the world below.

sentences.l: said · by · the-Osiris · Ani · I · the-egg · which-is-in · the-Great-Cackler
sentences.i: Said by the Osiris Ani: I am the egg which is in the Great Cackler.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḏd in in red. ḏd in wsir ꜣny as in Spell 61. wsir is the low seat (coded Q2, approximate) over the eye, with no god classifier, and ꜣny again has the seated man (A1). ink 'I' as before; Budge's footnote mark after it points to a variant from another papyrus, which is not read as text. swḥt 'egg' is the folded cloth s (S29), the chick w, the wick ḥ and t, with the egg as classifier. imyt 'which is in' is the crossed planks im with m and t: the nisba of m 'in', feminine to agree with swḥt, its y not written. ngg-wr begins with water n and the jar-stand g written twice: ngg 'cackle'. Then come a goose lying down (G38) over the mouth r, and the seated god. wr 'great' is normally written with the swallow (G36), as in line 3. Here the bird is printed as a goose, and with the r below it it is read wr; the goose is also the bird the name describes. Budge prints both parts as one group (Neḳeḳ ur), and they are kept as one name, 'the Great Cackler'. The Great Cackler is a goose of the beginning of things, and the dead man speaks as the egg it carries.

sentences.l: (iw) · have-guarded-I · place · this · great · which-opened(?) · Geb · to · the-earth
sentences.i: I have guarded this great place which Geb opened(?) to the earth.
sentences.n: iw, the reed and the chick, opens the statement and is not translated. sꜣw·n·i is the seated herdsman with his stick (A47), the sign of sꜣw 'guard', with w as complement, the low hooked sign (U15) as classifier, water n and ·i: the sḏm·n·f, 'I have guarded'. The low sign is the classifier, not the arm ꜥ: there is no ꜥ in the word (Budge: sau-nà). st 'place' is the seat (Q1) with t and the house as classifier (Budge: àuset). twy 'this' is t, the coil w (Z7) and two reeds: the feminine demonstrative, agreeing with st. Budge's line numeral 2 stands before ꜥꜣt 'great', the column ꜥꜣ (coded O29, approximate) with t, the arm ꜥ as complement and the roll, feminine again. wpt is the horns wp (F13, approximate) with p as complement and t, then crossed sticks (Z9), the classifier of parting and crossing, and the man with hand to mouth (A2) as classifiers: the same group as wpt 'the judging' in Spell 18. Budge reads àpt ('proclaimed'), but the horns write wp, as in Spell 17, where he reads them àpt too. The word is taken as the relative form of wpi 'open, part', feminine to agree with st, with gb as its subject: 'which Geb opened'. The man with hand to mouth is the classifier of speech, which wpi can take in the sense 'pronounce, judge'. gb 'Geb' is the goose gb (G38) with b and the seated god (Budge: Seb). r tꜣ is r with the strip of land over grains (coded N16, approximate). wpi X r Y can also mean 'part X from Y', so the clause may instead be 'which Geb parted from the earth'. The sense is not certain. Budge's footnote here gives a variant from another papyrus and is not read as text. Geb is the earth itself, and the place he opens may be the way out of the earth.

sentences.l: live-I · lives-it · am-strong-I · live-I · breathe-I · the-air
sentences.i: I live, and it lives; I am strong, I live, I breathe the air.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes nḫḫt·i; read nḫt·i. The placenta ḫ is written twice, and the word meant is nḫt 'be strong' (water n, ḫ and t). Its classifier is the low hooked sign (U15), printed for the arm with a stick, the classifier of force that nḫt takes (as sḫm in Spell 61); it is not the arm ꜥ, and there is no ꜥ in the word. The seated man ·i is restored by Budge. A verb nḫḫ 'grow old' has the same letters without the t, and is classified with the bent old man; the t and the classifier of force speak for nḫt (Budge: neχeχt-à, 'I grow strong'). ꜥnḫ·i 'I live' is the sign ꜥnḫ (S34) with n and ḫ as complements and ·i: the sḏm·f. ꜥnḫ·s has the bolt for ·s 'it', feminine: the egg, or the place of the line before. ssn·i is the folded cloth s twice and water n, with the nose (D19) and a long bar (coded Y1, approximate, taken as the roll) as classifiers, and ·i: ssn 'breathe' (Budge: sesen-à, 'I smell'). nfw 'the air' is written as in the title, the same word as 'breath'. The spell's title is fulfilled here: the dead man breathes.

sentences.i: I am Wedja-aab(?); I have gone round about his egg.
sentences.n: ink 'I' as before. Budge's line numeral 3 follows it. Budge prints two groups after it, utā and aāb, with the English 'Utcha-aāb', a name, and they are joined here as one word, wḏꜥ-ꜣꜥb (q re-indexed). The first part is the chick w, the cobra ḏ with the arm ꜥ under its head, the sign wḏꜥ (Aa21) and the walking legs. It is wḏꜥ 'judge, separate', spelled as in Spell 125; the legs are not explained. The second part is the vulture ꜣ and the foot b crossed by the arm ꜥ in one ligature, then a cup (coded W10, approximate) and a long loaf on a mat (coded R4, approximate). The seated god after it is restored by Budge. ꜣꜥb is not known; its two classifiers, both approximate, may point to a vessel or an offering, but that is a guess. The name is not understood, and the reading is doubtful. rr·n·(i) is a long loop (coded V10, approximate) and r, with the walking legs and water n. It is the sḏm·n·f of rr 'go round', as in Spells 17 and 18, its subject ·i not written. ḥꜣ 'behind, about' is the papyrus clump ḥꜣ (M16) with ꜣ and a small head (D1), as before. A water n follows that adds nothing clear and is not translated. It may be the genitive, with ḥꜣ taken as a noun, 'the back of'. swḥt·f 'his egg' is written as in line 1, with ·f. Whose egg is meant is not said, perhaps the Great Cackler's. The dead man is both the egg and the one who guards it.

sentences.i: I have dawned(?) at the moment of the one great of strength, Seth.
sentences.n: bkꜣ·n·i is the foot b, the raised arms kꜣ (D28) with ꜣ as complement, and a large plain circle (coded N5, approximate) as classifier, the sun, then water n and ·i: the sḏm·n·f. With the sun as classifier the word would be bkꜣ 'morning, grow light', so 'I have dawned', but that gives no clear sense here. The same letters spell bkꜣ 'be pregnant', which the egg of the lines before might suggest, though the classifier is the sun. Budge's 'I have destroyed (?)' is his own guess, and he marks it doubtful. The reading is uncertain. ꜣt 'moment' is a large animal head, coded E25 (the hippopotamus), approximate. It is taken as the hippopotamus head that writes ꜣt (Gardiner F3), with t as complement and the sun (N5), the classifier of time (Budge: at). In Spell 147 the same head follows t and ꜣ as a classifier; here no ꜣ is written, and the head carries the sound. A noun of time can stand without a preposition: 'at the moment'. wr 'the great one' is the swallow wr (G36, approximate) with a seated figure as classifier. pḥty 'of strength' is restored by Budge in full: p and t, the hindquarters pḥ (F22, approximate), two strokes y and a leopard's head (F9, approximate). wr pḥty, an adjective followed by the noun that says in what respect, is 'great of strength', a common epithet. ꜣt wr pḥty is the direct genitive, 'the moment of the one great of strength', and stẖ stands after it, naming him. stẖ 'Seth' is the bolt s, t and the pool (coded N37, approximate) for ẖ, with the seated god (Budge: Set). Seth's 'moment' may be his hour of rage, which the speaker has outlived; the sense is doubtful.

sentences.i: O sweet one of the Two Lands, who are among the provisions, who are in the lapis lazuli, may you keep watch over the one who is in his nest, the child who comes forth to you.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes ḏfsꜣ and ḫsbꜣ; read ḏfꜣw and ḫsbḏ. In the first the pintail duck sꜣ (G39) stands where the vulture ꜣ is expected, in the second the vulture stands where the cobra ḏ is expected. The signs keep their own values; the classifiers (bread, and the grains of a mineral) allow no other words. i 'O' is the reed with a standing man raising one arm (coded A26, approximate), the gesture of calling. nḏm is the twisted pod nḏm (coded M29, approximate) with m and the roll: 'sweet, pleasant', here the adjective used as a noun, 'the sweet one'. tꜣwy, the strip of land (N16, approximate) written twice for the dual, 'the Two Lands', Egypt, follows as a direct genitive. Budge's 'thou who makest pleasant' would need the causative snḏm, which is not written. imy 'who is in' is the crossed planks im with m and two strokes y, three times in this line. ḏfꜣw 'provisions' is the cobra ḏ, the viper f and the duck (for ꜣ), with a long loaf (coded X4, approximate) and plural strokes, its w not written. ḫsbḏ 'lapis lazuli' is ḫ, the bolt s, b and the vulture, with three grains and plural strokes; the blue stone may stand for the sky (Budge: 'the blue'). sꜣw·tn is the herdsman (A47) with ꜣ as complement (the bird is printed as a vulture), the low hooked sign (U15; there is no ꜥ in the word) and ·tn: the sḏm·f, 'may you guard'. r 'over'. sšt·f 'his nest' is the bolt s, the pool š (coded N37, approximate), two oblique strokes (not read), a nest with young birds (G48), t, a stroke and ·f. It is sš 'nest' (Budge: seśet-f), the t written as it stands. nḫn 'the child' is n, ḫ and n with a seated child, hand to mouth (A17), and the seated man. pr·f 'he comes forth' is the sḏm·f of pri after the noun it describes, 'who comes forth'. Budge prints r and tn as two groups, and they are joined as r·tn 'to you', r with the suffix ·tn (q re-indexed). The words of address are singular, but ·tn is plural. Either several beings are hailed by one set of names, or the number is a slip; as it stands, 'you' is plural. The dead man, as the child in the nest, asks the beings of the sky to watch over him. After this unit Budge prints Spells 55 and 56 from other papyri (Naville's edition and the papyrus of Nebseni), which are not on Ani's papyrus.
